# Welcome to didgpu {.unnumbered}

Modern difference-in-differences work is rarely a single estimator and a
single model. It is a workflow: choose an identification strategy, estimate a
panel with treatment timing that may be staggered or heterogeneous, check for
pre-trends, run bootstraps, compare sensitivity analyses, and often revisit
trade-offs when the data become large enough to make the naive approach feel
impossible.

That is where `didgpu` comes in.

`didgpu` is a GPU-capable R package for applied DiD research that brings six
published estimator families under one consistent interface. It is built for
researchers who want the credibility of the modern DiD literature without the
pain of stitching together multiple packages, each with its own output
conventions, startup costs, and idiosyncratic bootstrap behavior.

The package is designed around three principles:

- Credibility: the estimators are implemented against the reference
  literature and cross-checked against the established R packages that define
  the benchmark for applied work.
- Speed: when inference is the bottleneck, the optional CUDA backend can
  reduce the cost of cluster-bootstrap workloads on supported hardware.
- Reliability: long-running bootstrap fits can be checkpointed and resumed,
  avoiding the all-too-common loss of an entire overnight run.

A GPU is not required. Every estimator has a pure-R and Rcpp fallback, and
`didgpu` is designed to run cleanly in both CPU-only and CUDA-enabled
settings. The package is also built to behave appropriately in CRAN-style
validation environments, where GPU support is not assumed.

## Why didgpu exists

If you have used modern DiD methods in practice, you already know the
frustration: the method is compelling, but the implementation story is often
fragmented. Some estimators live in one package, some in another, some are
only available as research code, and many demand custom workflows for
bootstrap inference, sensitivity checks, and repeated runs.

`didgpu` consolidates the main modern DiD families into a single package with
one interface, one set of conventions, and one place to compare results on the
same panel.

That matters because the applied research question is often not “which one is
best in the abstract?” but “which estimator is best suited to this design,
and can I estimate it at scale without rewriting my workflow?”

## The six estimator families

| Family | Function | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Dynamic, heterogeneity-robust DiD | `didgpu()` | de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2024) |
| Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered DiD | `didgpu_cs()` | Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) |
| Fixed-effects counterfactual (FEct, IFEct, MC) | `didgpu_fect()` | Liu, Wang, and Xu (2024); Athey et al. (2021) |
| Instantaneous DID_M (non-absorbing binary) | `didgpu_did_static()` | de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020) |
| Continuous treatment dose-response | `didgpu_cs_continuous()` | Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and Sant'Anna (2024) |
| Continuous treatment, no stayers | `didgpu_did_continuous()` | de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2024) |

This is not merely a package of aliases. Each estimator is implemented as a
first-class workflow, with its own identification logic, diagnostic tools, and
inference machinery. The goal is not to force one estimator into one shape,
but to make the comparison across settings easier, faster, and more
transparent.

The [Choosing an estimator](chapters/02b-choosing-estimator.qmd) chapter walks
through the decision process for a given application.

## What makes it practical

### Speed where it matters

Cluster bootstrap inference is usually the dominant computational cost in
modern DiD workflows. For large panels, the pure-R implementation is already
credible and flexible, but the optional CUDA backend brings a substantial
reduction in the time needed for repeated inference.

In benchmarked settings, the GPU path has been observed to achieve:

- roughly 10x to 100x speedups for cluster-bootstrap workloads
- roughly 5x to 30x speedups for the per-cell DID kernel

Performance depends on panel size, number of covariates, and the number of
bootstrap replicates. See `BENCHMARKS.md` for the hardware and panel
configurations behind these numbers.

### Resilience for long runs

Long cluster bootstraps fail for reasons that are all too familiar: out-of-memory
errors, machine restarts, interrupted jobs, or a process killed by a scheduler.
Instead of forcing a complete restart, `didgpu` can checkpoint every completed
bootstrap replicate to disk and resume from the last completed state.

This is more than a convenience feature. It is a practical reliability layer for
applied work where an overnight job should not become a lost day.

### Numerical credibility

`didgpu` is designed around numerical parity with the reference packages in the
DiD ecosystem. Under matched settings, point estimates align to machine
precision with packages such as `DIDmultiplegtDYN`, `did`, and related
implementations. Analytic standard errors agree closely, and bootstrap
standard errors match up to simulation noise.

This is important because performance is not the only bar. A faster estimator is
not useful if it drifts materially from the benchmark software researchers use
for validation.

## How to read this book

- **Part I (Getting Started).** Install the package, run your first
  estimator, and work through the decision guide for which estimator fits
  your application.
- **Part II (Estimators).** One chapter per estimator family, covering the
  function signature, identifying assumptions, options, and a worked example.
- **Part III (Advanced).** GPU setup, checkpointing, reproducibility,
  sensitivity analysis, and bootstrap variants.
- **Part IV (Reference).** Methodology notes, FAQ, and changelog.

## Cite

If `didgpu` played a role in your published work, please cite both the
package and the relevant method papers:

```{r citation, eval=FALSE}
citation("didgpu")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
The package print method prints the citation for the method paper
corresponding to the estimator you ran. Each estimator family has a
one-line `citation()` entry.
:::

## Status

`didgpu` is actively maintained and available from the project repository:
<https://github.com/JoshuaAmmons/didgpu>.

Numerical correctness is re-tested on every push with a randomized
comparative-testing suite. The current status badge:

```
Last full sweep: ~17,000 informative comparisons, 0 failures
Main 1285-case battery (all backends, all flags): clean
Bit-for-bit equivalence with DIDmultiplegtDYN 2.3.x across the
weighted-by-flag matrix
```
